=======

debian 12

<https://hestiacp.com/install.html>

wget <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hestiacp/hestiacp/release/install/hst-install.sh>

bash hst-install.sh --clamav no --spamassassin no --webterminal yes

Filemanager fix:

Bash

cd /usr/local/hestia/web/fm/backend/Services/Session/Adapters/

mv SessionStorage.php SessionStorage.php.bak\
curl -fsSLm20 https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hestiacp/hestiacp/refs/heads/main/install/deb/filemanager/filegator/backend/Services/Session/Adapters/SessionStorage.php -o SessionStorage.php

4\. Ensure the permissions are correct:

Bash

chown hestiaweb:hestiaweb SessionStorage.php

Redis
-----

Update your package list to ensure you get the latest version:

Bash

apt update

Install the Redis server:

Bash

apt install redis-server -y

Enable Redis to start automatically on server reboots, and start the service now:

Bash

systemctl enable redis-server

systemctl start redis-server

Verify that Redis is running. It should respond with PONG:

Bash

redis-cli ping

Open the Redis configuration file:

Bash

vim /etc/redis/redis.conf

Search for the maxmemory directive (you can use Ctrl+W in nano to search). Uncomment it and set it to around 256MB (which is plenty for a single WooCommerce store):

Plaintext

maxmemory 256mb

Right below that, find or add the maxmemory-policy directive and set it to allkeys-lru:

Plaintext

maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru

Save and exit (Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X).

Restart Redis to apply the changes:

Bash

systemctl restart redis-server

Install the Redis PHP extension for your specific PHP version (replace 8.2 with the version you found in Step 1):

Bash

apt install php8.3-redis -y\
(Note: If you are using PHP 8.1, the command would be apt install php8.1-redis -y, and so on).

Restart the PHP-FPM service to load the new extension:

Bash

systemctl restart php8.3-fpm

Now that the server is ready, you need to connect WordPress to Redis.

1.  Log in to your WordPress wp-admin dashboard.

2.  Go to Plugins -> Add New and search for Redis Object Cache (by Till Krüss).

3.  Install and Activate the plugin.

4.  Go to Settings -> Redis in the WordPress menu.

5.  Click the "Enable Object Cache" button.

-   Note: The plugin should instantly connect to the Redis server via the default 127.0.0.1:6379 address. You will see a green "Connected" status.\
Config
========

PHP-FPM profiles 
-----------------

1\. Copy a Default Template

Navigate to Hestia's PHP-FPM template directory and duplicate the template for the specific PHP version your domain uses. The naming convention is strict: it must follow the YOURNAME-PHP-X_Y.tpl format.

Bash

cd /usr/local/hestia/data/templates/web/php-fpm/

cp PHP-8_3.tpl tuned-PHP-8_3.tpl

####  The Process Manager (pm)

This dictates how PHP-FPM handles spinning up and shutting down worker processes.

|

Mode

 |

How it Works

 |

Best For

 |
|

ondemand

 |

Starts processes only when traffic hits. Kills them when idle.

 |

Low-RAM servers, shared hosting (like HestiaCP defaults), or sites with sporadic traffic.

 |
|

dynamic

 |

Keeps a minimum number of workers alive at all times. Spawns more as traffic increases, up to a limit.

 |

Most standard websites. Balances RAM usage with fast response times.

 |
|

static

 |

Keeps a fixed, maximum number of processes running 100% of the time.

 |

High-traffic, dedicated servers where RAM is plentiful and maximum performance is required.

 |

#### 2\. The Core Variables

Depending on the pm mode you chose above, these variables control the boundaries.

-   pm.max_children (Applies to: All modes)

-   What it is: The absolute maximum number of concurrent PHP processes allowed.

-   TLDR: If this is 10, your site can handle 10 simultaneous PHP scripts running at the exact same millisecond. Request 11 gets queued.

-   pm.start_servers (Applies to: Dynamic)

-   What it is: How many workers to spin up the moment PHP-FPM restarts.

-   TLDR: A baseline to handle immediate traffic after a reboot.

-   pm.min_spare_servers (Applies to: Dynamic)

-   What it is: The minimum number of idle workers kept alive waiting for a request.

-   TLDR: Prevents lag. If a traffic spike hits, these workers are already warm and ready.

-   pm.max_spare_servers (Applies to: Dynamic)

-   What it is: The maximum number of idle workers. If more are idle, FPM kills the extras.

-   TLDR: Prevents idle workers from hoarding your RAM.

-   pm.process_idle_timeout (Applies to: Ondemand)

-   What it is: How many seconds a worker must sit doing absolutely nothing before it is killed.

-   TLDR: Usually set to 10s. Too low = CPU waste from constant respawning. Too high = RAM waste.

-   pm.max_requests (Applies to: All modes)

-   What it is: How many requests a single worker process serves before it automatically self-destructs and is replaced by a fresh clone.

-   TLDR: Set to 500 or 1000. This is your safety net against 3rd-party plugin memory leaks.

#### 3\. The "Max Children" Cheat Formula

Never guess your pm.max_children. Use your server's math to find the ceiling.

1.  Find out how much RAM a single PHP process uses on your site (usually 30MB - 60MB for WordPress). Let's say 50MB.

2.  Find out how much RAM you have available specifically for PHP (Total Server RAM - OS/DB/Webserver RAM). Let's say you have 1000MB free.

3.  Divide Free RAM by Process Size:  1000 / 50 = 20.

4.  Your absolute safe pm.max_children is 20. Set it a little lower (e.g., 15) to leave a safety buffer.\
max power settings for 8 vcpu 16 gb single woocommerce hestiacp:

pm = static\
pm.max_children = 60\
pm.max_requests = 1000\
and for it's stagings:

pm = ondemand\
pm.max_children = 5\
pm.process_idle_timeout = 10s\
pm.max_requests = 500

Nginx direct wp rocket serve
----------------------------

#=========================================================================#

# WP Rocket cache proxy template (nginx front -> Apache/PHP-FPM backend)  #

#=========================================================================#

server {

        listen      %ip%:%proxy_ssl_port% ssl;

        server_name %domain_idn% %alias_idn%;

        error_log   /var/log/%web_system%/domains/%domain%.error.log error;

        ssl_certificate     %ssl_pem%;

        ssl_certificate_key %ssl_key%;

        #ssl_stapling        on;

        #ssl_stapling_verify on;

        if ($anti_replay = 307) { return 307 https://$host$request_uri; }

        if ($anti_replay = 425) { return 425; }

        include %home%/%user%/conf/web/%domain%/nginx.hsts.conf*;

        set $rocket_file "/wp-content/cache/wp-rocket/$host${uri}index-https.html";

        # ---- Bypass: blank the path so try_files falls through to WordPress ----

        if ($request_method !~ ^(GET|HEAD)$) {

                set $rocket_file "/rocket-no-cache";

        }

        if ($query_string != "") {

                set $rocket_file "/rocket-no-cache";

        }

        if ($request_uri ~* "/(wp-admin/|wp-login\.php|wp-cron\.php|xmlrpc\.php|wp-json/|index\.php|feed/|sitemap.*\.xml|.*\.php)") {

                set $rocket_file "/rocket-no-cache";

        }

        #if ($http_cookie ~* "(wordpress_logged_in_|wp-postpass_|comment_author_|woocommerce_items_in_cart|woocommerce_cart_hash|wp_woocommerce_session_)") {

        #        set $rocket_file "/rocket-no-cache";

        #}

        if ($http_cookie ~* "(wordpress_logged_in_|wp-postpass_|comment_author_)") {

                set $rocket_file "/rocket-no-cache";

        }

        location ~ /\.(?!well-known\/|file) {

                deny all;

                return 404;

        }

        location / {

                root %sdocroot%;

                # static assets straight off disk (your original behaviour)

                location ~* ^.+\.(%proxy_extensions%)$ {

                        try_files  $uri @fallback;

                        root       %sdocroot%;

                        access_log /var/log/%web_system%/domains/%domain%.log combined;

                        access_log /var/log/%web_system%/domains/%domain%.bytes bytes;

                        expires    max;

                }

                # page requests: serve cached HTML if present, else WordPress

                try_files  $rocket_file @backend;

                access_log /var/log/%web_system%/domains/%domain%.log combined;

        }

        # cache miss / bypass -> normal WordPress backend

        location @backend {

                proxy_ssl_server_name on;

                proxy_ssl_name $host;

                proxy_pass https://%ip%:%web_ssl_port%;

        }

        # fallback for missing static files

        location @fallback {

                proxy_ssl_server_name on;

                proxy_ssl_name $host;

                proxy_pass https://%ip%:%web_ssl_port%;

        }

        location /error/ {

                alias %home%/%user%/web/%domain%/document_errors/;

        }

        proxy_hide_header Upgrade;

        include %home%/%user%/conf/web/%domain%/nginx.ssl.conf_*;

}

OP Cache tuning
---------------

Log into your HestiaCP SSH or Dashboard and ensure your PHP settings (php.ini) are tuned to use your massive RAM:

For Websites (PHP-FPM): This is the one you will edit 99% of the time to affect your live sites. /etc/php/8.3/fpm/php.ini

For Command Line (CLI): This controls PHP when you run scripts directly from the SSH terminal or via Cron jobs. /etc/php/8.3/cli/php.ini

Ini, TOML

opcache.enable=1

opcache.memory_consumption=512  ; Raise this to 512 or 1024 if you have plenty of RAM

opcache.max_accelerated_files=50000

opcache.validate_timestamps=1\
HestiaCP Server Tuning (MySQL/MariaDB)
----------------------------------------

By default, HestiaCP installs a generic MySQL/MariaDB configuration meant for small blogs. For a store doing €60k/month, MariaDB needs more memory allocated to its buffer pool so it can keep your active WooCommerce data in RAM instead of reading from the disk.

1.  SSH into your server and open the MariaDB config:

2.  Bash

vim /etc/mysql/mariadb.conf.d/50-server.cnf

1.

2.  Look for innodb_buffer_pool_size. On a standard Hestia setup, it might be set very low (e.g., 128M).

3.  If your server has 8GB of RAM, you should increase this to 4G or 5G (roughly 50-60% of total server RAM if it's a dedicated web/DB server).

4.  Plaintext

innodb_buffer_pool_size = 4G

1.

2.  Save and restart MariaDB:

3.  Bash

systemctl restart mariadb

1.

Unattended Upgrades
===================

Debian 12 has a fantastic built-in tool for handling security patches silently in the background. This ensures your OS dependencies (like curl, OpenSSL, or core libraries) are patched against zero-day exploits without you lifting a finger.

Install and Enable:

Bash

apt update

apt install unattended-upgrades apt-listchanges -y

dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades

Note: When the prompt appears, select "Yes" to automatically download and install stable updates.

Verify Configuration: Open the configuration file to ensure it is only targeting security updates (which rarely break servers) and not major software version bumps.

Bash

vim /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades

comment out the non security updates:\
![](data:image/png;base64,)

Attended upgrades
=================

### How to handle updates for Hestia and Web Packages

1\. HestiaCP Control Panel Updates Hestia actually has its own built-in automatic update engine specifically designed not to break your web server.

-   You can turn this on in the Hestia Web UI -> Server (Gear Icon) -> Updates -> Enable Automatic Updates.

-   This ensures the control panel itself gets patched automatically without relying on Debian's upgrade tool.

2\. PHP, Nginx, and MariaDB Updates (Manual is best) For the software actually serving your WooCommerce stores, you should update these manually during a scheduled maintenance window. Once a week (or twice a month), simply SSH into your server and run:

Bash

apt update && apt upgrade -y

Because you already set up unattended-upgrades for the OS, this manual command will only pull down updates for PHP, Nginx, MariaDB, and Redis. Once it finishes, you can load up your WooCommerce checkout page to verify everything is still working perfectly.

Daily Malware Scanning: Linux Malware Detect (Maldet)
=====================================================

Since you disabled ClamAV during the HestiaCP installation to save RAM (a smart move for performance), you can use Maldet. It is specifically designed to find PHP backdoors, darkmailers, and web-shells in shared hosting environments.

Installation:

Bash

cd /usr/local/src/

wget http://www.rfxn.com/downloads/maldetect-current.tar.gz

tar -xzvf maldetect-current.tar.gz

cd maldetect-*

bash install.sh

Configuration:

Bash

vim /usr/local/maldetect/conf.maldet

Update these crucial settings:

-   email_alert="1" (Turn on alerts)

-   email_addr="you@yourdomain.com" (Set your email)

-   quarantine_hits="1" (Automatically move malware out of the public folder)

-   quarantine_clean="1" (Try to clean injected malicious code from core files)

Automated Daily Scans: The installer automatically creates a daily cron job at /etc/cron.daily/maldet. However, by default, it scans all user home directories. To make it faster, ensure it only scans the public web directories of your Hestia users. You can run a manual scan anytime with:

Bash

maldet -a /home/*/web/*/public_html/

Server Monitoring: Netdata
==========================

Netdata is the gold standard for real-time, per-second monitoring. It is lightweight and will show you exactly what is eating your CPU or RAM during a traffic spike or WooCommerce import.

Installation (Kickstart Script):

Bash

wget -O /tmp/netdata-kickstart.sh https://get.netdata.cloud/kickstart.sh && sh /tmp/netdata-kickstart.sh

Firewall Configuration: By default, Netdata runs on port 19999. HestiaCP has a strict firewall enabled out of the box, so you need to open this port.

1.  Log into your HestiaCP Web UI.

2.  Go to Server (Gear Icon) -> Firewall.

3.  Click Add Rule.

4.  Set Action to ACCEPT, Protocol to TCP, Port to 19999, and name it "Netdata".

5.  Save the rule.

You can now view your live dashboard by visiting http://YOUR-SERVER-IP:19999.

Regular Maintenance & Backups
=============================

Server tuning is only half the battle. Regular maintenance ensures you don't wake up to a crashed server because the disk filled up with error logs.

1\. Log Rotation (Built-in but check it) Hestia automatically rotates logs, but high-traffic Woo stores can generate massive Nginx access logs. Keep an eye on /var/log/nginx/ and /var/log/apache2/ (if using Apache backend) to ensure they are being compressed properly.

2\. Off-Site Backups (Mandatory) Do not rely solely on local Hestia backups. If the server dies, the local backups die with it.

-   Go to HestiaCP Web UI -> Server -> Configure -> Backups.

-   Set up a remote storage provider. Backblaze B2 (via SFTP/Rclone) or Amazon S3 are the cheapest and most reliable for this.

3\. Replace WP-Cron with System Cron Since you have WP-CLI set up and working, completely disable the unreliable web-based WordPress cron. Edit the site's wp-config.php:

PHP

define('DISABLE_WP_CRON', true);

Add a cron job in the HestiaCP UI for that specific user to run WP-CLI every 5 minutes:

Bash

/usr/local/bin/wp cron event run --due-now --path=/home/USER/web/DOMAIN/public_html/

Security stuff for nginx
========================

### The HestiaCP Solution: Custom Web Templates

Instead of creating a nginx.ssl.conf_security file for every single domain, the "Hestia Way" is to bake your security rules directly into a Custom Web Template.

Once you create this custom template, it appears in your HestiaCP Web UI dropdown. You just select it when adding a new WooCommerce site, and the security rules are automatically applied!

Here is how to set it up perfectly:

1\. Copy the Default Template Assuming you are running the standard Nginx + PHP-FPM stack, navigate to the template directory and duplicate the default WordPress template. You must copy both the HTTP (.tpl) and HTTPS (.stpl) versions.

Bash

cd /usr/local/hestia/data/templates/web/nginx/php-fpm/

cp default.tpl wp-secure.tpl

cp default.stpl wp-secure.stpl

2\. Inject Your Security Rules Edit both of your new files. Let's start with the SSL version (which handles 99% of your traffic):

Bash

vim wp-secure.stpl

Look for the server { block and scroll down just past the SSL certificate definitions. Paste your security block right there, before the other location blocks start:

Nginx

    # ... (SSL definitions above) ...

    # --- START CUSTOM SECURITY RULES ---

    location ~ /\.(?!well-known\/) {

        deny all;

        access_log off;

        log_not_found off;

    }

    location ~* (?:\.(?:bak|conf|dist|fla|in[ci]|log|psd|sh|sql|sw[op])|~)$ {

        deny all;

        access_log off;

        log_not_found off;

    }

    location = /xmlrpc.php {

        deny all;

        access_log off;

        log_not_found off;

    }

    if ($http_user_agent ~* (SemrushBot|AhrefsBot|MJ12bot|DotBot|PetalBot|MegaIndex|HTTrack|masscan)) {

        return 403;

    }

    # --- END CUSTOM SECURITY RULES ---

    location / { ...

Save the file, then repeat the exact same process for wp-secure.tpl (the HTTP version).

3\. Apply the Template via the Hestia UI Now, you never have to touch the SSH terminal for domain security again!

1.  Log into your HestiaCP dashboard.

2.  Go to the Web tab and Edit your target WooCommerce domain.

3.  Check the Advanced Options box.

4.  In the Web Template (Nginx) dropdown, you will now see wp-secure as an option. Select it!

5.  Save.

Hestia will instantly rebuild the Nginx configurations for that specific domain using your new hardened template. Whenever you migrate a new site to this server, just select the wp-secure template, and the site is locked down from second one.
